lines.text: Welcome to JavaScript Demystified.
Today's topic is closures.
Closures have a reputation for being confusing.
But by the end of this video, you will see that a closure is just one simple idea.
Let's start with a puzzle.
Here is a function called [makeCounter|make counter].
Inside, it creates a variable named count, starting at zero.
Then it returns a small function, which adds one to count, and gives back the result.
We call [makeCounter|make counter] once, and keep the returned function in a variable called counter.
Then we call counter, three times.
Here is the strange part.
[makeCounter|make counter] has already finished, so its variable count should be gone.
So, what do you think gets printed?
One. Two. Three.
The counter still remembers count, even though [makeCounter|make counter] finished long ago.
That memory is called a closure. Let's see how it works.
First, we need one small idea: scope.
Scope decides which variables a piece of code is allowed to see.
Think of a function as a room.
Variables created inside are the things inside that room.
Code inside the room can use them.
But code outside cannot see in. If we try, JavaScript throws a reference error.
Rooms can be nested.
A function written inside another function sits in a room, inside a bigger room.
The inner function can look outward, through the walls, into every room around it.
This is called lexical scope.
Lexical simply means: where you write the code decides what it can see.
Watch how the engine finds the variable user.
It checks the inner room first, and does not find it.
So it checks the next room outward, and finds it there.
Now greeting. Not in inner. Not in outer.
So the engine keeps going, and finds it in the global room.
And the code prints: Hello Sam.
Here is what the engine really does.
Every time a function runs, it creates a small record, called a lexical environment.
It holds the function's local variables, plus a link to the environment outside it.
And here is the key.
When a function is created, it remembers the environment where it was born.
Picture a backpack.
The function packs its surrounding variables, and carries them wherever it goes.
A function, together with its backpack, is a closure.
In JavaScript, every function is a closure, created at the moment the function is created.
Now let's replay the puzzle in slow motion.
We call [makeCounter|make counter].
The engine creates an environment, with count set to zero.
Next, the inner function is created. Its backpack points to that environment.
[makeCounter|make counter] returns the inner function, and finishes.
Normally, its environment would be thrown away.
But the returned function still points to it, so the environment stays alive.
Now we call counter. It looks for count, and does not find it locally.
So it follows its backpack, and finds count in the surviving environment.
It adds one. Count is now one.
Call it again, and count becomes two. Again, and it becomes three.
The same count, every time. That is how counter remembers.
Every call to [makeCounter|make counter] creates a brand new environment.
So counters made separately do not share anything.
We make counter A, and counter B.
Call A twice, and it prints one, then two.
Now call B. What do you think it prints?
One. B has its own count.
One more important detail.
A closure keeps a link to the variable itself, not a copy of its value.
Here, we change message after the function is created.
When we call show, it prints the new value: bye.
It always sees the current value.
So what are closures good for?
First: private data.
Here, balance lives inside [createAccount|create account]. Nothing outside can touch it directly.
The only way to change it is through the functions we chose to share.
Deposit fifty, and the balance becomes one hundred fifty.
But asking for account dot balance gives undefined.
The variable is safely hidden.
Second: function factories.
[makeAdder|make adder] takes a number, and returns a new function that remembers it.
[add5|add five] always adds five.
[add10|add ten] always adds ten.
Each one carries its own backpack.
Closures also power timers, click handlers, and callbacks, every single day.
Now, the most famous closure trap.
This loop starts three timers. Each one prints i.
What do you think it prints?
Three, three, three.
Why? Because var creates only one variable i, shared by the whole loop.
By the time the timers fire, the loop has finished, and i is three.
All three functions share the same i.
The fix is let.
With let, every round of the loop gets its own fresh i.
So each function gets its own backpack.
Now it prints zero, one, two.
One last thing to remember.
A closure keeps its variables alive for as long as the function itself is alive.
That is usually exactly what you want.
But if a function holds on to something big, and you no longer need it, let go of the function.
Then the environment can be cleaned up, and the memory freed.
Let's recap.
One. A closure is a function, together with the variables around the place where it was created.
Two. It keeps a live link to those variables, not a copy.
Three. Use closures for private data, function factories, and callbacks.
And in loops, use let instead of var.
That's closures, demystified. Thanks for watching.
Next time: the mysterious keyword, this.
